content: Dock3, also referred to as Dedicator of Cytokinesis 3, MOCA (modifier of cell adhesion), or PBP (presenilin-binding protein), is a large intracellular protein with a molecular weight of approximately 180 kDa. It plays a critical role in intracellular signaling pathways. Dock3 belongs to the DOCK-B subfamily within the DOCK family of guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs), which are responsible for activating small G proteins. Specifically, Dock3 functions as an activator of the small G protein Rac1. Dock3 was initially identified through a screening process aimed at finding proteins that interact with presenilin, a transmembrane protein known to harbor mutations associated with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease. Dock3 is predominantly expressed in neurons, with its expression being most prominent in the cerebral cortex and hippocampus. Dock3 is a member of a broad class of proteins known as guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs), which facilitate cellular signaling by activating small G proteins. In their inactive state, G proteins are bound to guanosine diphosphate (GDP). Activation of these proteins requires the exchange of GDP for guanosine triphosphate (GTP), a process mediated by GEFs. Dock3 shares a similar domain structure with Dock180, a member of the DOCK-A subfamily and a prototypical member of the DOCK family. Dock3 and Dock180 exhibit approximately 40% sequence similarity. Due to its structural similarity to Dock180, Dock3 is predicted to interact with a comparable set of binding partners, although this has not yet been fully confirmed. Dock3 contains an N-terminal SH3 domain, which in Dock180 is known to bind ELMO, a family of adaptor proteins that facilitate the recruitment and efficient GEF activity of Dock180. Additionally, Dock3 has a C-terminal proline-rich region, which in Dock180 interacts with the adaptor protein CRK. The guanine nucleotide exchange factor activity of Dock3 is specifically directed toward Rac1, a small G protein. Dock3 has not been shown to interact with Rac3, another Rac protein expressed in neuronal cells. This lack of interaction may be attributed to Rac3’s predominant localization in the perinuclear region. Interestingly, Rac1 and Rac3 appear to have distinct and opposing roles in neuronal cells. Activation of Rac1 by Dock3 leads to cytoskeletal reorganization in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells and primary cortical neurons. Furthermore, Dock3-mediated Rac1 activation induces morphological changes in fibroblasts and regulates processes such as neurite outgrowth and cell-cell adhesion in B103 and PC12 cells. The potential involvement of Dock3 in neurological disorders was first suggested when it was found to bind presenilin, a transmembrane enzyme involved in the production of beta-amyloid (Aβ). The accumulation of Aβ is a critical step in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer’s disease. In brain samples from Alzheimer’s patients, Dock3 has been observed to redistribute and associate with neurofibrillary tangles. Additionally, a mutation in the Dock3 gene has been identified in a family exhibiting a phenotype resembling attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
